questions.question: Why are AI dev environments generally harder to reproduce than typical web application environments?
options: AI code is written in a slower programming language
They have more interdependent layers — OS, GPU driver, CUDA/ROCm toolkit, framework, and model libraries must all be compatible versions
AI applications never use version control
Web applications don't run on operating systems
questions.explanation: AI environments add a GPU driver, CUDA/ROCm toolkit, and deep learning framework layer beneath the application code, each of which must be version-compatible with the ones above and below it.

questions.question: A model produces slightly different outputs on a new GPU box, but the code runs without any errors. What failure class does this describe?
questions.explanation: Silent numerical drift occurs when code runs successfully but produces subtly different results due to environment differences like floating-point rounding or different kernel implementations — dangerous because it can pass casual testing while breaking reproducibility.

questions.question: Engineering reports a delay because 'the model gives different results on the new GPU box.' Which question best helps a TPM assess this as a real, known issue rather than a vague excuse?
options: Can we just use a different programming language?
Do we log an environment fingerprint (CUDA version, framework version, GPU type) alongside training runs, and is environment mismatch one of the first hypotheses being tested?
Why do we need GPUs if they cause bugs?
Can we skip testing and ship anyway?
questions.explanation: Environment fingerprinting and treating environment mismatch as a standard early hypothesis are established practices for diagnosing this well-known AI engineering failure mode quickly and credibly.
